answer.label: Not Plato — a modern line from Bill Bullard
answer.authorDates: American educator · former Dean of Faculty, San Francisco University High School
answer.sourceLine: This is a pop–psychology slogan, not Plato. It appears in none of Plato’s dialogues; Wikiquote lists it as misattributed ↗ and traces it no further than a graduation speech by educator Bill Bullard at San Francisco University High School (online by July 2007), whose fuller line runs “the highest form of knowledge… is empathy.” Bullard himself credited George Eliot — an attribution Wikiquote notes is likewise unsupported.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Bill Bullard, commencement speech, San Francisco University High School
Online by July 2007; catalogued as misattributed by Wikiquote

source.excerpt: Opinion is really the lowest form of human knowledge; it requires no accountability, no understanding. The highest form of knowledge… is empathy, for it requires us to suspend our egos and live in another’s world.
trail: Wikiquote’s Plato page ↗ files this under Misattributed, calling it “a very common online pop-psychological slogan” traced “no further than a graduation speech… given by Bill Bullard, who within the speech attributes it to George Eliot,” adding that “the attribution to Eliot seems likewise to be false.”

An early attestation is Ben Casnocha’s July 2007 blog post ↗, which quotes Bullard’s speech: “Opinion is really the lowest form of human knowledge… The highest form of knowledge, according to George Eliot, is empathy.”
The fuller passage is widely catalogued under Bullard’s name, e.g. on Goodreads ↗ — never sourced to any Platonic dialogue.
source.excerptNote: Bill Bullard’s commencement remarks, as quoted online in 2007. The circulating “Empathy is the highest form of knowledge” is a compressed paraphrase of this passage — and neither the passage nor the slogan is Plato’s.
source.rightsNote: The wording originates in Bill Bullard’s commencement speech documented online in 2007, so as a modern (post-1930) text it is in copyright to its author. There is no pre-1931 — or ancient — source for this phrasing to place in the public domain.

author.name: Bill Bullard
author.heading: Who actually said it
author.metaLine: American educator · former Dean of Faculty, San Francisco University High School
author.bio: Bill Bullard was an educator and former Dean of Faculty at San Francisco University High School. His commencement remarks — contrasting opinion as the “lowest form” of knowledge with empathy as the “highest” — circulated online from 2007 and are the earliest documented source of the saying. Bullard credited the thought to novelist George Eliot, but no such passage has been found in her work, so the phrasing is best traced to Bullard himself.

misattribution.heading: How Plato got the credit
misattribution.intro: A tidy, uplifting maxim with no home in any dialogue — exactly the kind of line that drifts onto Plato’s name online. Here the paper trail actually leads somewhere specific.

items.why: The phrase appears in none of Plato’s dialogues; Wikiquote ↗ files it under Misattributed as “a very common online pop-psychological slogan.”
The line is traced to Bullard’s graduation speech at San Francisco University High School, quoted online by July 2007 ↗: “The highest form of knowledge… is empathy.”
Within the speech Bullard credited the idea to George Eliot, but Wikiquote ↗ notes “the attribution to Eliot seems likewise to be false” — no such passage is known in her writing.

misattribution.truthLine: Best evidence: a modern line by educator Bill Bullard (documented 2007), not Plato — and the secondary credit to George Eliot is unsupported too, per Wikiquote ↗.

context.heading: Why it caught on
lead: The slogan works because it flatters a modern intuition — that feeling-with others is a form of understanding — and Plato’s name lends it the gravity of antiquity. But Plato’s epistemology prized reason and the Forms; he had no concept matching the modern word “empathy,” which only entered English in the early 20th century.

Bullard’s original was a rhetorical ladder — opinion at the bottom, empathy at the top — aimed at graduating students. Stripped to five words and re-tagged “Plato,” it became a caption-ready maxim, which is how most people now meet it.
context.pull: Plato had no word for “empathy” — the term is barely a century old.
